input:
Staffing decisions can have a significant impact on both service quality and operating costs, and the dispatch office considered here provides a useful illustration of the trade-offs involved. The office currently employs 4 full-time staff, and over the course of last year, overtime accounted for 16% of paid hours, which is a substantial proportion by any standard. In response to this situation, consideration has been given to replacing half of the overtime — equivalent to 8% of paid hours — with one additional hire. The fully loaded cost of such a hire would be $70k per year.

However, it is important to note that the overtime in question is not spread evenly throughout the year. Instead, it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, which means that demand for additional hours is particularly intense during certain periods and considerably lower at other times. A new hire, by contrast, would be paid for the full year, regardless of whether the peaks are in progress or not. This creates a potential mismatch between the pattern of costs and the pattern of demand, underscoring the complexity of the decision. Ultimately, decision-makers will need to weigh the $70k annual cost of the additional hire against the overtime expenditure it would displace, taking into account the seasonal profile described above, in order to arrive at a balanced and sustainable outcome.
target:
Replacing half of the dispatch office's overtime with one additional hire costs $70k per year, fully loaded. The office has 4 full-time staff. Overtime ran at 16% of paid hours last year, so the swap removes overtime equal to 8% of paid hours and replaces it with a salaried post paid across the whole year.

The case turns on the shape of the overtime, not its total. The overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and that share is an average over the year: the rate inside the peaks stands above the average, and the rate outside them stands below it. Within the peaks, the hire absorbs work that overtime would otherwise cover. Across the rest of the year, the post is an addition to the existing staff, paid at its full-year cost whether or not peak work is present, with no overtime saving set against it in those months. A post bought for the peaks is therefore paid for at the year's length, while the overtime it displaces is bought only in the weeks that generate it.

The comparison as stated is incomplete in one respect: the cost of the hire is given and the cost of the overtime it replaces is not, so the net effect on the pay bill cannot be computed from these figures. What the figures establish is the commitment the office takes on, a fixed yearly cost set against overtime that arises only in two seasonal peaks. A decision on the swap needs the overtime cost for the peak periods, stated at the same yearly scale as the $70k.
